issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may decline to quash an order made without jurisdiction when doing so would restore an unlawful payment or determination.
material_facts: The Member of the Board of Revenue directed steps to recover compensation paid in excess of the amount legally payable.
The governing Act specified the relevant authorities and their powers but did not confer power on the Board of Revenue to issue that direction.
Quashing the direction would have removed the recovery notice and revived the higher compensation assessment, which the Court considered unlawful.
issues.conclusion: The direction was upheld notwithstanding the Board Member’s lack of jurisdiction, because setting it aside would have restored an unlawful order for excess compensation.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the discretionary nature of extraordinary judicial review and relied on Gadde Venkateswara Rao v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1966 SC 828, and Mohammad Swalleh v. IIIrd Additional District Judge, Meerut, AIR 1988 SC 94: a court may refuse relief against an order made without jurisdiction when granting relief would revive an invalid or unlawful order.

predicates.administrative_compensation_recovery_pro: The matter is a proceeding concerning recovery of compensation paid under a statutory compensation assessment.
predicates.challenged_order_made_without_authority: An authority issued the challenged direction without power under the governing law.
predicates.quashing_would_restore_unlawful_compensa: Setting aside the challenged direction would revive a compensation determination or payment that the court considers unlawful.
predicates.court_may_refuse_to_quash_challenged_ord: The court may decline to set aside the challenged order.

issues.definition: When an authority’s order is challenged in a compensation recovery proceeding, the court may leave it in place despite lack of authority if quashing it would restore unlawful compensation.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment that affects substantive compensation rights and contains no express or necessarily implied retrospective operation applies prospectively.
material_facts: The amendment changed the method for determining compensation for mines and minerals and affected the proprietor’s substantive compensation rights.
The amendment stated that it would come into force at once but did not state that it would operate retrospectively.
The compensation entitlement was to be determined under the law applicable when compensation was payable.
issues.conclusion: The amendment applied prospectively, so the unamended compensation provision governed the compensation in this case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the presumption against retrospectivity for legislation affecting substantive rights, relying on Garikapatti Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhury, [1957] SCR 488, and the principles in Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra, [1994] 4 SCC 602. It also relied on Union of India v. C. Rama Swamy, [1997] 4 SCC 647, in rejecting the argument that substitution alone made the amendment retrospective. The relevant provisions were Section 1(2) and Section 6 of the Bihar Land Reforms (Validation and Amendment) Act, 1974, and Sections 24 and 25 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950.

predicates.statutory_compensation_proceeding: The matter concerns compensation determined under a statute.
predicates.amendment_affects_substantive_rights: A statutory amendment changes a party’s substantive entitlement to compensation.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent_shown: The amendment contains no express or necessarily implied indication that it applies to past or pending entitlements.
predicates.amendment_applies_prospectively: The amendment governs only prospectively and does not displace the law applicable to the earlier entitlement.

issues.definition: In a statutory compensation proceeding, an amendment affecting substantive rights applies prospectively when the amendment shows no intention to operate retrospectively.

issues.legal_issue: Where compensation is fixed by agreement, a party who accepts the assessment without objection cannot later demand that the compensation dispute be referred to a tribunal.
material_facts: The proprietor accepted the final compensation assessment roll without protest and notified the compensation authority that he would not object to it.
The governing provision allowed compensation for mines and minerals to be fixed by agreement, with a tribunal reference available if no agreement was reached.
The proprietor later sought a higher rate and claimed that the compensation should be referred to a tribunal.
issues.conclusion: The acceptance of the compensation assessment without objection constituted an agreement, and the proprietor could not require a tribunal reference for determination of the compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 25(4)(a) of the unamended Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, compensation could be fixed by agreement; under Section 25(4)(b), reference to a tribunal arose only if no agreement was reached. The Court held that acceptance of the final assessment roll without protest established agreement and foreclosed the tribunal route.

predicates.statutory_mines_compensation_proceeding: The matter concerns statutory compensation for mines or minerals.
predicates.final_assessment_accepted_without_object: The recipient accepted the final compensation assessment without objecting to it.
predicates.tribunal_reference_requires_absence_of_a: The governing process provides for tribunal determination only when the parties have not agreed on compensation.
predicates.party_cannot_demand_tribunal_reference: The party cannot later require the compensation dispute to be determined by a tribunal.

issues.definition: In statutory mines compensation proceedings, a recipient who accepts the final assessment without objection cannot demand a tribunal reference when tribunal determination is available only in the absence of agreement.

issues.legal_issue: A final compensation assessment cannot be reopened after payment unless the statutory conditions for correction or discovery of further vested interests are met.
material_facts: Compensation had been paid after the final assessment roll was accepted.
There was no discovery that further interests of the proprietor had vested in the State.
The statutory grounds for correction before payment, including a bona fide mistake or a change in entitlement through succession or transfer, were not present.
issues.conclusion: The compensation officer could not use the statutory correction or fresh-assessment powers to revise the final assessment after payment in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 30 of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, permitted specified corrections before payment, including correction for a bona fide mistake or as a result of succession or transfer. Section 30-A permitted a fresh assessment roll if further interests of the intermediary were discovered to have vested in the State. Neither provision authorized reopening on the facts of this case.

rule.if: statutory_compensation_assessment_proceeding and compensation_already_paid and no_qualifying_correction_ground and no_further_vested_interest_discovered

predicates.statutory_compensation_assessment_procee: The matter concerns a final assessment of compensation under a statutory scheme.
predicates.compensation_already_paid: The compensation assessed has already been paid to the recipient.
predicates.no_qualifying_correction_ground: No statutory ground for correcting the assessment, such as a qualifying mistake or change in entitlement, is present.
predicates.no_further_vested_interest_discovered: No additional interest of the recipient is discovered to have vested in the State after the assessment.
predicates.officer_cannot_reopen_final_assessment: The compensation officer cannot reopen or revise the final assessment.

issues.definition: A compensation officer cannot reopen a paid final assessment when no statutory correction ground exists and no further vested interest has been discovered.

issues.legal_issue: A party who accepts a final compensation assessment cannot later challenge it on the ground that a required preliminary procedural step was omitted.
material_facts: The proprietor accepted the final compensation assessment roll.
He later argued that the prescribed preliminary procedure involving a draft in the required form had not been followed.
The Court held that, having accepted the final assessment, he could not raise that procedural objection.
issues.conclusion: The challenge based on noncompliance with the preliminary procedure was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered Rule 18(2) and the prescribed preliminary form, but held that acceptance of the final assessment prevented the proprietor from later relying on the alleged procedural omission.

predicates.statutory_compensation_assessment_procee: The matter concerns an assessment of compensation under a statutory procedure.
predicates.final_assessment_accepted: The party accepted the final compensation assessment.
predicates.later_challenge_based_on_omitted_prelimi: The party later challenged the assessment because an earlier procedural step was allegedly omitted.
predicates.party_cannot_raise_procedural_objection: The party cannot rely on that alleged procedural omission to challenge the accepted assessment.

issues.definition: In a statutory compensation assessment proceeding, a party who accepts the final assessment cannot later challenge it for an allegedly omitted preliminary procedural step.
